studies.Reference: Zinc supplement use and risk of aggressive prostate cancer: a 30-year follow-up study.
studies.Authors: Zhang Y, Song M, Mucci LA, Giovannucci EL
studies.comparison_type: ≥75 mg/day supplemental zinc versus never use
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Men reported their zinc supplement use at baseline and biennially thereafter.

sample_size.excerpt: A total of 47,240 men from the Health Professionals Follow-up Study were followed from 1986 to 2016.

cases.excerpt: During a median follow-up of 28.3 years, we documented 6,980 incident prostate cancer cases including 1,053 lethal and 1,143 aggressive.

effect_size.excerpt: However, compared to never-users, men who used supplement zinc more than 75 mg/day were at higher risk for lethal (HR: 1.76, 95% CI: 1.16-2.66, P<sub>trend</sub> = 0.001) and aggressive prostate cancer (HR: 1.80, 95% CI: 1.19-2.73, P<sub>trend</sub> = 0.006). Similarly, men who took supplemental zinc for 15 or more years had a higher risk for lethal (HR: 1.91, 95% CI: 1.28-2.85, P<sub>trend</sub> <0.001) and aggressive prostate cancer (HR: 1.55, 95% CI: 1.03-2.33, P<sub>trend</sub> = 0.004).

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 3 studies yielded an overall effect size of 1.26 (95% CI: 1.0–1.59), suggesting that mineral supplements is associated with a higher risk of prostate cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 60.50%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
